How to Search Public Records in Georgia

Georgia has 159 counties, a statewide land records index, and one of the shortest response deadlines in the country. Learn how to find business, court, and property records and use the Open Records Act.

Key takeaways

  • ✓The GSCCCA offers statewide indexes of land records, liens, and UCC filings.
  • ✓The Open Records Act requires a response within three business days.
  • ✓Fees are limited: the first quarter hour is free, copies are capped at $0.10 per page, and estimates over $25 must be shared.

In this guide

  1. Business Records: the Secretary of State
  2. Court Records: Superior, State, Magistrate, and Probate Courts
  3. Property Records: the Superior Court Clerk and the GSCCCA
  4. The Georgia Open Records Act
  5. Tips for Georgia Searches

Georgia has 159 counties, more than almost any state except Texas, and its records are spread across local offices. Two things make Georgia easier to research than it first appears: a statewide index of land records and a short, specific deadline in its Open Records Act. This guide explains where to look for business, court, and property records and how to make a request.

Business Records: the Secretary of State

Corporations, LLCs, and similar entities are registered with the Georgia Secretary of State's Corporations Division, which provides an online business search. A record normally shows the entity name, type, status, registered agent, and filing history, and the annual registration shows whether a company is current. Always compare the registered agent and principal office with what a business has told you.

Court Records: Superior, State, Magistrate, and Probate Courts

Georgia has several trial-level courts. Superior courts handle felonies and major civil cases, state courts hear misdemeanors and civil cases, magistrate courts handle small claims and certain minor matters, and probate courts handle estates and related issues. The clerk of the superior court in each county keeps the files for that court and, importantly, also keeps the county's real estate records. Search systems vary by county, and some counties require an account or fee for document images.

  • Identify the county where a case was filed and which court handled it.
  • Check magistrate and probate courts separately, because they often keep their own records.
  • Federal cases are filed in the Northern, Middle, or Southern District of Georgia and are searched through PACER.

Property Records: the Superior Court Clerk and the GSCCCA

Deeds, liens, and related real estate documents are recorded with the clerk of the superior court. The Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority (GSCCCA) maintains statewide indexes of real estate records, liens, and UCC filings, so you can search across counties from one place. Some features require fees or an account, so check the site for what is available without charge. County boards of tax assessors set property values, and county tax commissioners collect taxes, so valuation and payment questions go to different offices.

The Georgia Open Records Act

The Georgia Open Records Act (O.C.G.A. 50-18-70 and following) gives the public the right to inspect and copy records of state and local agencies. Agencies designate an open records officer, and the details are specific.

  1. Three business days: an agency must produce the records, or respond about them, within a reasonable time that does not exceed three business days. If some records are available sooner, it should produce those.
  2. If records are not ready: the agency must give a description of the records and a timeline for producing them within the three days.
  3. If it denies a request: it must cite the specific legal exemption, by code section, subsection, and paragraph.
  4. Fees: there is generally no charge for the first quarter hour of search time, copies are limited to $0.10 per page, and an agency that expects costs above $25 must tell you the estimate within the three days. Advance payment can be required for larger amounts.
  5. No new records: an agency is not required to create a report or compilation that did not already exist when the request was made.

If you have a problem, the Attorney General's Open Government Mediation Program offers informal mediation, particularly for disputes involving local governments, and you can also file a civil action in superior court.

Tips for Georgia Searches

  • Use the GSCCCA index to find which county holds a deed or lien, then request copies from that county's clerk.
  • Make requests in writing and say clearly that you are making them under the Open Records Act.
  • Keep a record of when you sent a request. The three-business-day clock starts when the agency receives it.
  • Ask for an estimate if a large request might run over $25.

Procedures and fees can change, so confirm them with the agency before you rely on them.
